<a id="add-schedule-fields"></a>

### Add schedule fields

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** add columns to these schedules, and say which ones could not be added and why.

Adds named columns to every schedule handed in, and separates THREE OUTCOMES the version this was re-authored from ran together under one counter. Its own comment admitted the conflation - *"already present, or not addable to this schedule type"* - both landing in the same `notFound` tally as a genuine spelling mistake. Those are three different situations needing three different responses: | Outcome | What it means | What you do | |---|---|---| | `added` | the column is now there | nothing | | `alreadyPresent` | it was there before | nothing — **and this is not a failure** | | `notSchedulable` | that field cannot go on this schedule | pick a different field | | `unknownField` | no field of that name exists for this category | check the spelling — the real names come back | WHEN A NAME IS NOT FOUND, THE REAL NAMES ARE HANDED BACK. Schedulable fields are **category-specific and are not free text** - a name that works on a door schedule may not exist on a duct one. Nearly every miss is a spelling or a wrong-category assumption, and the list of what IS available is the answer to the question the caller is about to ask. A COLUMN IS NEVER ADDED TWICE. Two identical columns in a schedule is the same failure as two tags on one element: it looks plausible on screen and is wrong on the sheet. **VERSION 2 ADDS COMBINED COLUMNS, AND EDITS OR MOVES A COLUMN** (ADD_SCHEDULE_COMBINED_FIELD merged in): one column joining several parameters with a separator between each two - *"Type - Mark"* - a real field that follows the model; a part that does not resolve stops that column. With editExisting the column named is rebuilt where it stands, and position puts a column first, last, after or before another. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so a batch of columns across several schedules is one undo entry.

<a id="add-spot-elevations"></a>

### Add spot elevations

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-09 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** put the levels on these on the drawing.

Places a spot elevation on each element in one view - the annotation that puts a real height on a drawing, as opposed to a tag, which puts an identity on one. **WHICH FACE IS PICKED IS THE ANSWER, AND REVIT OFFERS THE WRONG ONE FIRST.** A floor hands back its BOTTOM face before its top. A fragment that takes the first planar face with a reference therefore annotates the SOFFIT and reports success - a plausible number, three hundred millimetres wrong, printed straight onto a sheet. This was found by running it: a 300 mm slab with its top at 0 was annotated -300.0 and reported as one placed, none skipped. **The face test has to be POSITIVE, and that is the subtle half.** Guarding with the absolute value of the normal's Z does NOT catch it, because the soffit's normal is -1 and its absolute value passes. The test is that the normal points UP. **So every candidate face is collected before one is chosen**, never first-one-wins, and the face wanted is asked for rather than assumed - top for a finished floor level, bottom for a soffit, and the report prints the height actually annotated on each element so a wrong face cannot hide behind a success count. **An element whose geometry yields no usable face reference is skipped and named.** A spot elevation needs a real geometric reference, not a point, and much of a model cannot give one. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="apply-color-fill-scheme"></a>

### Apply color fill scheme

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-23 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** colour the rooms, spaces or HVAC zones in a plan by one parameter with Revit's Color Scheme, and place its Color Fill Legend.

Colour-fills plans the way Revit's own Color Fill does it: sets the views' Color Scheme for one category - Rooms, Spaces, HVAC Zones, Areas, Ducts, Pipes, whichever the view takes - to one that colours by the parameter named, re-colours its rows - a band such as pastel, or one colour per value - and places Revit's Color Fill Legend in the view. Takes a view's Color Scheme off again too. "Colour the rooms by name" and "add a colour fill legend" are this. **NOT COLOR_BY_PARAMETER**, which paints overrides element by element; a scheme follows a renamed room by itself. **A SCHEME OTHER VIEWS SHOW IS COPIED, NEVER RE-COLOURED UNASKED.** A category with no scheme is refused. **ALL OF IT OR NONE OF IT.** Once anything is written, a failure rolls the whole request back. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="apply-view-filter"></a>

### Apply view filter

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-26 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** put that filter on this view and make it do something.

Adds a filter to a view and sets its whole row on the view's Visibility/Graphics Filters tab - Enable Filter, Visibility, Projection/Surface Lines and Patterns, Transparency, Cut Lines and Patterns, Halftone. The step after making a filter - without which the filter exists in the project and does nothing to any drawing. **Every control of the row, since version 2 (2026-09-28, FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-248).** The graphic ones come in `overrides`: line pattern, colour and weight; foreground and background pattern, colour and Visible tick; for the surface and for the cut; transparency, halftone. Patterns by the name Revit shows, or `solid`. `enabled` is the Enable Filter tick and `visible` the Visibility tick. `solidFill` puts Revit's solid fill on as the foreground pattern from this fragment's own code, so it works on an add-in that has not been restarted since the pattern keys were added to the parser. **A blank leaves it as it is.** With `keepOtherSettings` blank or true only what `overrides` sets changes, so "halftone the return air filter" keeps its colours. `keepOtherSettings=false` replaces the filter's whole override - the way to clear a colour or switch halftone, transparency or a Visible tick back to Revit's default, which a keep-mode call cannot do because those defaults are also values. `overrides=none` asks for no graphic change at all, for a call that only ticks or unticks. **Cut is never stamped where it cannot show.** When none of the filter's categories can be cut (`Category.IsCuttable`), Revit greys the Cut columns out and a cut value set anyway is stored and draws nothing. The cut half is left out and the answer says "cut not applicable to this filter's categories" and names them. **"Untick the filter" is two different ticks in Revit's own dialog** - Enable Filter and Visibility sit side by side. Unticking Visibility HIDES what the filter matches; unticking Enable Filter switches the filter off so its elements draw as if it were not there. Ask which is meant when the sentence does not say. **It works with either kind of filter.** A rule-based view filter and a saved selection filter are both looked up through the class they share, and a view does not care which it was handed. That is why one fragment serves both CREATE_VIEW_FILTER and UPDATE_SAVED_SET, whose mode "create" saves a set. **Projection and cut are BOTH set, always.** Revit does not derive one from the other, and setting only the projection is why a filter looks right in plan and shows the wrong colour the moment anything is cut. Found on a real model where twenty-six filters carried a projection colour and no cut colour. **Re-running it updates rather than fails.** A filter already on the view has its override and ticks rewritten, which is what somebody adjusting a colour actually wants - and the `summary` names each setting that changed, before and after, or says NOTHING CHANGED. **Hiding is done here too, and it is the same operation.** A filter set invisible hides everything it matches in that view - the ordinary way to take a discipline out of a drawing without deleting anything. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

Also takes detail-level, projection-line-weight, projection-line-pattern, surface-foreground-pattern, surface-foreground-colour, surface-foreground-visible, surface-background-pattern, surface-background-colour, surface-background-visible, cut-line-colour, cut-line-weight, cut-line-pattern, cut-foreground-pattern, cut-foreground-colour, cut-foreground-visible, cut-background-pattern, cut-background-colour, cut-background-visible, surface-colour and cut-colour. <a id="apply-view-template"></a>

### Apply view template

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** put a view template on these views.

Applies one view template to a set of views. The office's standard, applied the way it is meant to be applied — once, from a template — rather than by overriding each view by hand. **A view template LOCKS whatever it controls, and that is the whole point and the whole hazard.** Every setting the template includes stops being editable on the view. Graphic overrides somebody applied by hand are not deleted — they are overruled and become invisible and unreachable, which reads exactly like the work having been lost. **That makes this the fragment the grayout job has to route around.** Greying a background by category and then applying a template that controls V/G overrides silently discards the greyout. The order matters and neither call reports the conflict. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="assign-scope-box-to-view"></a>

### Assign scope box to view

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-14 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** put a named scope box on views, or take it off.

Puts a named Scope Box onto views - the view's own Scope Box property - or clears it. One scope box across a set of plans is how a drawing series keeps the same extent on every sheet without anybody dragging crop regions. **A SCOPE BOX CANNOT BE CREATED FROM CODE ON ANY RELEASE HERE**, and that is the honest half of this fragment. Revit exposes no create call for one. The box is drawn once by hand - View tab, Scope Box - and from then on this can put it on as many views as the drawing set needs, which is where the repeated work actually is. **CLEARING IS THE SAME OPERATION**, not a second one: an empty name writes the invalid id, which is what "None" in the properties palette holds. That matters because a view stuck on the wrong scope box crops wrong on the sheet and the fix is not obvious. **A SCOPE BOX IS NOT A CROP AND NOT A SECTION BOX**, and all three answer *"only show this part"*. A scope box is a NAMED, SHARED extent that many views obey at once and that also controls how far grids and levels reach. A crop belongs to one view. A section box cuts the 3D. Choosing the wrong one gives a drawing that looks right today and drifts the moment somebody edits one view. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="close-view-tabs"></a>

### Close view tabs

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-08 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** close the view tabs I have finished with, without losing the views.

Closes open view TABS in the active project. It deletes nothing: the views themselves stay in the Project Browser and can be reopened at any time. **CLOSING A TAB IS NOT DELETING A VIEW, AND THE WORDING HAS TO CARRY THAT.** *"Close the view"* and *"delete the view"* are one keystroke apart in a chat and a world apart in a model. This closes tabs only. DELETE_ELEMENTS is what removes a view, and it is a different, MODIFY-risk operation on purpose. **IT WILL NEVER CLOSE THE LAST OPEN TAB, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE SAFETY OF IT.** In Revit, closing the last open view of a project closes the PROJECT - and a project very likely has unsaved work in it. A request that would empty the tab bar is honoured as far as it safely can be and then stops, with the kept-back tab named. Losing somebody's unsaved model to tidy up their tabs is not a trade this fragment will make. **THE ACTIVE TAB IS THE ONE KEPT BACK** when the request would otherwise close everything, because leaving the user looking at the view they were already in is the least surprising place to stop. **A TAB THAT IS ALREADY CLOSED IS NOT A FAILURE.** It is reported separately from the ones that were closed, because "I asked for six and six happened" and "I asked for six, four were open" are different facts and merging them hides the second. Opens no transaction and needs none: it acts on the session, not the building. That is why it is EXECUTE rather than MODIFY.

|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes only what Revit shows - a selection, a zoom, a view (`EXECUTE`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **You say** | **view names** - a list - comma separated |
| **You get** | closed, closed names, findings |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2024 |
| **Capability** | `CLOSE_VIEW_TABS` |

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.
2. In a Claude chat, ask in your own words, for example *"close that view tab"*. Say the values under **You say** in the same sentence.
3. Revit shows the result. Nothing in the model changes.

Other ways to ask: *"close the views I am finished with"* · *"tidy up my open tabs"*

<a id="color-by-parameter"></a>

### Color by parameter

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** give every system its own colour in this view.

Gives every distinct value of one parameter its own colour in one view - colour by System Name, by Level, by Type, by anything the elements carry. The co-ordination picture: supply one colour, return another, chilled water a third, and which is which readable at a glance. **The colours are stepped evenly around the hue wheel, and there is no fixed palette.** The earlier library offered one and it carried the exact defect the hue stepping was written to fix: six colours repeating means the seventh system gets the first system's colour, and two runs on one drawing then look like one system. Even hue steps guarantee every group is visually distinct from every other however many groups there are, which a list of colours cannot. **The same request gives the same colours every time.** The earlier library re-rolled a random starting hue on each run "for variety". A drawing whose colours change every time it is produced cannot be compared to the one issued last week, and the person reading it has to re-learn the legend. Groups are sorted by their value and the hue runs from a fixed start, so the mapping is stable no matter what order the elements arrived in. **It is an override in ONE view and it changes nothing about the elements.** The model is untouched; another view is unaffected. RESET_GRAPHIC_OVERRIDES is how it is undone. **A blank value is its own group and is named as one.** Elements with nothing in that parameter are coloured together and reported as "no value" rather than left plain, because plain in a coloured drawing reads as "not part of this" instead of "nobody filled it in". **AN ELEMENT CARRYING THE NAME TWICE IS NOT COLOURED.** A shared or project parameter can be bound beside a built-in one of the same name, and Revit's lookup by name then returns one of them at random, in Autodesk's own words - so its colour would say a value nobody chose. Listed in `ambiguous`, and when every element handed in is one, nothing is coloured and `refused` says why (D-54 s3, FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-203). ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **view** - a view, by name - resolved BY NAME in Revit; a name matching twice is refused<br>**parameter name** - text<br>**colour band** - text |
| **You get** | coloured, legend, no value, wraps followed |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |
| **Capability** | `COLOR_BY_PARAMETER` |

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.
2. Select what it works on in Revit (elements) - or name it in the same request, and Heron finds it first.

Other ways to ask: *"give every system its own colour"* · *"colour these by level"*

<a id="copy-view-filters"></a>

### Copy view filters

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** put this view's whole filter set onto other views.

Copies the filters from one view onto other views - each filter WITH the override that makes it look like something and WITH its on/off state. The answer to *"I set the colours up on this plan, now put the same on the other twelve"*. **ADDING THE FILTER IS NOT COPYING IT, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE REASON THE FRAGMENT EXISTS.** `AddFilter` puts the filter on the view with EMPTY overrides - no colour, no line weight, nothing. The look lives in a separate object, and the on/off state in a third. Copy the filter alone and you get twelve views carrying the right filters and showing no change at all, which reads as the job not having run. All three are copied here, and the report says which of the three moved. **A VIEW GOVERNED BY A TEMPLATE WILL NOT TAKE ITS OWN FILTERS**, and that is the case a batch quietly loses. The template owns Visibility/Graphics. Such views are NAMED with their template, because the fix - copy onto the template instead - changes every view using it at once and is usually what was wanted. **It is not APPLY_VIEW_FILTER in a loop.** That one puts ONE filter on a view with an override the caller built. This reads a working view and replicates it, which is a different question: nobody copying a set knows what the twenty overrides on it are, and having to describe them would be the reason not to do it. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **You get** | views changed, filters applied |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |

<a id="create-3d-view"></a>

### Create 3D view

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** make a new 3D view.

Creates a fresh 3D view. The coordination view somebody makes to look at one problem, rather than disturbing a view that is on a sheet. **Creating and duplicating are different jobs and the words are the same.** `DUPLICATE_VIEWS` copies an existing view with its settings; this makes a new one from the template type, carrying none. Somebody who says *"make me a 3D view like that one"* wants the first. **The view family type is an input.** A project can carry several 3D view types with different templates and defaults attached, and which one is correct is an office convention, not something to infer (D-33). **It is a plain isometric and nothing more.** No section box, no isolation, no camera position. Those are separate capabilities on purpose — the view this makes is the thing they act on, and a fragment that did all four could not be re-used for any one of them. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

### Create area plan

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** make a new area plan view for this level, to place areas in.

Creates an area plan view for one level - the Gross Building or the Rentable plan that areas are placed and boundaries drawn in. **IT CLOSES A HOLE PLACE_AREAS LEFT OPEN.** Areas can only be placed in an area plan, and CREATE_PLAN_VIEW makes floor and ceiling plans only - so PLACE_AREAS and CREATE_AREA_BOUNDARY_LINES had nowhere to work in a project that had no area plan yet. **WHICH KIND IS NAMED, NEVER GUESSED.** Gross Building and Rentable are measured to different faces of a wall and give different totals; the kinds this model holds are listed when the name matches none. **ONE AREA PLAN PER LEVEL AND KIND IS MADE, NOT A SECOND.** An area plan that already exists for that level and kind is reported by name and nothing is made - two of one kind invite areas placed twice. **IT MAKES THE VIEW AND DRAWS NO BOUNDARY.** Revit's own dialog offers to draw boundary lines round the exterior walls; this does not, and says so. CREATE_ROOM_SEPARATION_LINES, with lineKind area, is that step. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="create-assembly-views"></a>

### Create assembly views

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-16 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** make the shop drawing views for this assembly.

Turns each assembly into its own set of shop-drawing views: a 3D orthographic, detail sections from the sides you ask for, a part list and a material takeoff. The prefabrication deliverable, which is otherwise a long manual sequence repeated per assembly. **AN ASSEMBLY IS THE ONLY THING IN REVIT THAT GENERATES ITS OWN DRAWINGS, AND THAT IS WHY THIS IS WORTH A FRAGMENT.** The views it makes are OWNED by the assembly: they show only its members, they orient to the assembly's own origin rather than to project north, and they follow it if it moves. Nothing built by hand reproduces that - a section drawn across an assembly is just a section. **THE ASSEMBLY HAS TO BE COMPLETE FIRST.** An assembly whose type is not settled refuses to make views, and the refusal is per assembly rather than fatal - a set of twenty usually has one that was left half made. **IT DOES NOT MAKE THE SHEET.** Revit can make one, and placing views on sheets is a job this library already does properly - with title blocks, positions and a naming convention that belong to the office rather than to this call. The views are created and named; the sheet is the next fragment. **IT DOES NOT RE-MAKE VIEWS THAT ARE ALREADY THERE.** Running it twice on the same assembly would otherwise leave two of everything, which on a prefabrication job means two drawings claiming to be the same part. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

**What it does:** draw a callout around this part of a view, enlarged.

Draws a callout over a rectangle of a parent view and makes the enlarged view it points at. **A callout is two things at once and that is what makes it useful.** It puts a marked boundary on the parent drawing AND creates a linked view at a bigger scale. Move the callout on the plan and the detail follows; the reference on the plan updates itself when the detail lands on a sheet. Drawing the two separately gets a detail that says nothing about where it came from. **The scale is separate from the boundary.** A callout drawn at the parent's scale shows nothing new - the whole point is to enlarge, and Revit does not choose that for you.

<a id="create-plan-view"></a>

### Create plan view

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** make the floor or ceiling plan for this level.

Creates a floor plan or a reflected ceiling plan for one level. **It closes a hole CREATE_LEVELS opens.** A level made through the API comes with no views - Revit's Level *tool* makes them, the level itself does not - so the modeller adds a level, looks in the Project Browser, sees nothing and concludes it failed. CREATE_LEVELS says so; this is the fragment that fixes it, and the pair is the whole job: *"add 4 more floors"* means levels **and** the plans to draw on. **Floor or ceiling is asked for, not assumed.** An MEP modeller adding a level usually wants both, and which one is wanted first is not something to guess: a reflected ceiling plan looks upward and shows different things, and handing somebody the wrong one wastes the trip.

<a id="create-room-elevations"></a>

### Create room elevations

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-11 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** make interior elevations looking out from inside a room.

Puts an elevation marker inside a room and creates up to four interior elevations from it - the toilet, the kitchen, the plant room walls, drawn looking outward from a point in the middle. **IT IS A DIFFERENT MECHANISM FROM CREATE_SECTION_VIEW, NOT A SPECIAL CASE OF IT.** A section is a line and a depth, cutting through the model. An interior elevation is a MARKER with up to four slots, each slot producing a view that looks at one wall from inside. Nothing about a section produces the little four-arrow symbol a drawing set expects, and asking for room elevations and getting sections is the mis-route this closes. **THE FOUR SLOTS POINT IN THE MARKER'S DEFAULT DIRECTIONS AND ARE NOT ROTATED TO FACE THE WALLS.** In a room square to the project axes that is right. In a rotated room the four views look at corners. The marker is an ordinary element and rotating it afterwards turns the views with it - said here because it is invisible until somebody puts the sheet together. **THE PLAN IT GOES IN IS PART OF THE REQUEST, NOT A GUESS.** The marker is visible in that plan and the elevations inherit its phase, so putting it in the wrong plan produces four views of the wrong phase's walls - which looks like a modelling problem and is not one. **The point is given in internal FEET.** A room's centre is arithmetic on its geometry and belongs to the caller (D-01) - READ_ROOM_GEOMETRY provides it. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

Creates a new section view cut through a set of elements, sized to contain them plus a margin the request supplies. **It exists because "create a section through this" resolved to SET_VIEW_SECTION_BOX**, which crops a 3D view to a box. Both have the word *section* in them and they are not the same job in any respect: one makes a new drawing that can go on a sheet, the other hides part of a view that already exists. That is what somebody means by *"a section through this"*. The other orientation gives a long elevation, which is a legitimate drawing and never the one that sentence asks for.

<a id="create-view-filter"></a>

### Create view filter

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** a rule that finds elements by a parameter value and colours whatever matches.

Creates a filter that tests one parameter - or several, all or any of them (version 2) - applies it to a view, and colours whatever the rule matches. Version 3: the parameter by its name, and an operator in front of the value when it is not equals - "does not contain Level 1". **A filter matches; it does not remember.** Whatever satisfies the rule is caught, including work modelled next week - so a reissued drawing stays correct with nobody touching it. That is the whole reason to set one up. **The rule is a project-wide object.** Creating it puts it in the project's filter list, available everywhere and applicable to the whole set later. It outlives the view it was made for. **Several at once, and on no view when that is the job** (version 4). Each filter gets its own name and one value, all on the same categories and the same parameter - "Supply Air, Return Air and Exhaust Air on System Classification, for air terminals and ductwork". Leave the view and the colour out and they are made on no view, the way a modeller sets up a standard in Manage > Filters. One category that cannot take the rule stops the whole call and is named; a name already a filter is skipped and named, never overwritten. Each new filter is read back from Revit - its categories, its rule as held, and how many elements it catches today. **Or one per value, read off the elements** (version 5): each distinct value of the parameter becomes its own filter in its own colour, the blank ones too.

<a id="create-view-template-from-view"></a>

### Create view template from view

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** save the way this view is set up as a reusable view template.

Captures a view's current settings - its scale, detail level, discipline, phase, visibility and every graphic override on it - as a new named view template. IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE LIBRARY COULD APPLY A STANDARD AND NOT MAKE ONE. Views get set up by hand, one at a time, and the office standard ends up living in whichever plan somebody got right. This is the call that turns that view into the standard. **IT DOES NOT PUT THE NEW TEMPLATE ON THE VIEW IT CAME FROM, UNLESS ASKED.** Capturing a view's settings and being governed by them are two different requests, and only the second one locks the view. A template applied back to its source view makes every setting on it read-only from that moment - the exact state `REMOVE_VIEW_TEMPLATE` exists to undo. Revit's own *Create Template from Current View* does not apply it back either. The earlier library always applied it and said so in a comment; making it a decision the caller states, and reporting which happened, is deliberate. **A DUPLICATE NAME DOES NOT LOSE THE TEMPLATE.** Revit refuses a name another view or template already holds. When it does, the template is still created and keeps the name Revit gave it, and the refusal is reported with that name - because a fragment that threw the template away over a naming clash would have destroyed the captured settings, which are the expensive part. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** make an elevation looking straight at this wall, from outside or from inside.

Places an elevation marker in front of one straight wall, turned so its view looks square at the wall's face - from the exterior side or the interior side - and makes that elevation. The facade, the plant room wall, the riser wall a services drawing needs. **CREATE_ROOM_ELEVATIONS LOOKS IN THE MARKER'S DEFAULT DIRECTIONS**, so in a rotated building its views look at corners. A view per internal workset would bury the four that matter under thirty that do not. **A NON-WORKSHARED MODEL HAS NO USER WORKSETS AT ALL**, so it is said plainly rather than producing nothing and looking broken - which is the same output as a model whose worksets are all empty, and a different problem. **A VIEW NAME MUST BE UNIQUE AND REVIT THROWS ON A CLASH.** Existing names are collected first and a workset whose view already exists is skipped and named, so re-running this after adding one workset does not fail on the nineteen that were already done. **VISIBILITY IS SET PER VIEW, NOT BY A FILTER.** Each view shows its own workset and hides the rest through the view's own workset visibility, which is what a modeller then toggles by hand if they want two at once. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="diagnose-visibility"></a>

### Diagnose visibility

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-08 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** why is this element not showing in this view.

Says whether an element is actually shown in a view, and when it is not, **which of the reasons applies**. *"Why can I not see my ducts"* is one of the most expensive questions in Revit, because there are at least eight unrelated answers and no single place to look: the element is hidden, its category is off, a view filter excludes it, it is outside the view range, outside the crop, wrong phase, wrong design option, or on an unloaded workset. A modeller checks them one at a time and usually in the wrong order. **The ground truth is asked FIRST, and it is not a guess.** A collector scoped to the view returns what the view actually contains. Everything after that is explaining a fact rather than predicting one — which is the difference between this and a checklist. **It reports EVERY cause it finds, not the first.** Two causes at once is routine — a category switched off in a template *and* the element hidden by somebody — and fixing one leaves it still invisible, which is how the second hour goes.

<a id="duplicate-views"></a>

### Duplicate views

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** make copies of these views, plain or with the detailing, or as dependents - a legend under a new name, or a view template when asked.

Duplicates every view handed in, one of three ways, and hands back the ids of what was made so the next fragment can rename them, apply a template to them or place them on sheets. THE THREE WAYS ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE and the caller must choose: Duplicate the view alone. Annotation and detail items are NOT copied WithDetailing the view and everything drawn on it AsDependent a dependent view that stays tied to its parent's crop

Revit is asked FIRST whether each view can be duplicated that particular way, because the answer differs per option - a view can be duplicable plainly and refuse to become a dependent. Asking per option rather than per view is the difference between a clean skip and an exception. EACH VIEW IS TRIED ON ITS OWN. The version this was re-authored from wrapped the whole loop in one try, so one awkward view rolled back thirty-nine good duplicates. Under Golden Rule 16 the transaction belongs to the caller, so a throw let out of here would abort work this fragment never saw. Catching per view and reporting the id is both safer and more useful. The returned id is resolved back to a real view before it is counted. Every fragment here reports what HAPPENED rather than what was asked for, and an id that does not resolve is not a duplicated view. A VIEW TEMPLATE IS NOT DUPLICATED ON THE PLAIN PATH (version 2) and is reported in notDuplicated, so a template is never copied by accident. **Version 3: a legend under a new name, and a template when asked.** One view copied takes `newName`, read back, and a name Revit refuses is said. A legend copied is told it is on no sheet yet - a legend can sit on many sheets at once - and with nothing handed in, a project with no legend is told that Revit's API cannot make the first one. A view template is copied only when asked for - by name in `templateName`, or with `copyTemplates` - through CopyElements, because View.Duplicate cannot copy one; Revit's suffixed name for the copy is read back and the copy is not renamed here. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so duplicating forty views is one undo entry.

<a id="find-dates-in-views"></a>

### Find dates in views

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** where in this model has somebody typed a date, and in which view.

Finds every date typed into a text note ANYWHERE in the model and reports it with the view it was typed in. Read-only, and it scans the whole document rather than a selection. **IT EXISTS BECAUSE `EXTRACT_DATES_FROM_TEXT` ANSWERS A DIFFERENT QUESTION, and answering this one with that fragment would invent dates.** That one reads the notes ON a sheet and attributes each date TO that sheet, which is right for revision work. But a plan can be placed on five sheets, and a date typed inside that plan belongs to the plan. Rolled up to sheets it becomes five dates that nobody wrote. So every date here carries the view it was found in, and nothing is attributed upward. **THE ANSWER IS "WHERE", NOT JUST "WHAT".** A date on its own is not useful - the question behind it is always which drawing is out of date, or which view still says last month. So a date that appears in four views is reported once with all four named, rather than four times. **A SHEET IS A VIEW AND IS INCLUDED, and labelled as one.** Leaving sheets out would make this an incomplete answer to "where is this date written", and mixing them in unlabelled would make it a confusing one. A sheet reads as `M102 - Plan HVAC L2 (SHEET)`, a view as `Level 1 (FloorPlan)`. **A NUMERIC MONTH IS REFUSED, and that is the same rule the other fragment uses on purpose.** `03-04-2026` is 3 April in Qatar and 4 March in America. Two fragments reading one note and reporting different dates would be worse than either being wrong alone, because nothing would say which to believe. The parser here is the same one, and the finding says so when nothing is found. **A DATE IN A PARAMETER IS NOT THIS FRAGMENT'S BUSINESS.** Revit can already schedule and filter those. `READ_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS` reads them. What is invisible to every schedule in the model - and so worth turning into data - is the date somebody typed by hand. **VERSION 2 can read the sheets alone.** `sheetsOnly` reads only text typed ON a sheet, every sheet, nothing selected - a note inside a plan placed on it is counted and not read; `onlySheetsGiven` reads only the sheets handed in, never guessed from a selection, and names what is not a sheet. Every date then comes back once, oldest first, in one uncapped line with its sheets, and `datesFound` gives each date's sheet ids. Version 1's proof no longer describes the code and is kept as a record; the card is DRAFT until it is proved again.

| **You get** | dates found, view names, views with dates, findings, unique date count, date list, sheets with date count |

<a id="find-overlapping-tags"></a>

### Find overlapping tags

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-16 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** the tags are printing on top of each other in this view.

Finds annotation that PRINTS ON TOP OF other annotation in one view - tag over tag, text over a symbol, a keynote buried under a room tag. The drawing check that catches what nobody sees on screen at 200% and everybody sees on the printed A1. Read-only; it moves nothing. **It measures in paper millimetres, which is the only unit this question has.** Whether two tags clash depends entirely on the scale the view prints at - the same two tags are clear at 1:50 and merged at 1:200. Every figure here is converted through the view's own scale, so the answer is what comes out of the plotter rather than what the model happens to look like. **It projects onto the view's own paper axes, not onto world X and Y.** The earlier library compared model X against model Y, which is right in a plan and wrong in every section and elevation - a view looking along X has all its annotation at one X, so every box overlaps every other and the report is worthless exactly where a section is busiest. The boxes are projected onto the view's right and up directions instead, which is the same test in a plan and the correct one everywhere else. **Touching is not overlapping**, and how much counts is asked for. Two boxes sharing an edge are legible; two sharing half their area are not. **A bounding box is bigger than the ink**, so this over-reports slightly and says so. Two boxes can overlap while the visible characters do not touch. The opposite error costs a reissued drawing; this one costs thirty seconds of looking. **Tags over the drawing are found too (version 2)** - a door or window tag sitting on the wall poche in a plan, a tag a model or detail line runs through, a tag over a dimension's figure. A dimension is judged by where its figure sits, never by its box, which is the whole string, witness lines and all, and would overlap almost everything inside its own extent.

| **You get** | findings, overlapping, pairs, over model |

<a id="find-untagged-elements"></a>

### Find untagged elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-08 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** which of these already have a tag in this view, and which do not.

Splits a set of elements into the ones already tagged in one view and the ones not. It answers a real question on its own - *"which ducts have not been tagged"* is a drawing check somebody does before issuing - and it is the piece that hands TAG_ELEMENTS_IN_VIEW only the untagged ones. **It exists because the dependency graph said it had to.** TAG_ELEMENTS was written taking `alreadyTagged` as an input and nothing on disk could produce one, so `tests/test_graph.py` reported it as an action nothing can feed: a composition that cannot be assembled, however well each half compiles. The alternative was to mark that input as coming from the request, which would have made the graph quiet and the problem permanent - nobody can type a list of already-tagged element ids. **Tags are counted PER VIEW, because that is what a tag is.** The same duct is routinely tagged on the coordination plan and untagged on the section, and both are correct. A model-wide answer would report it tagged and the section would be issued bare.

<a id="find-views"></a>

### Find views

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-08 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** the real views or schedules in this model, narrowed by type, by name, by whether they are on a sheet or have a template.

Answers "which views" for everything that acts on views - applying a template, duplicating, placing on a sheet, exporting. It is the filter half of that whole family of jobs, which is why it is one fragment rather than a lookup copied into each of them (D-45). THE TRAP IT EXISTS FOR. Asking Revit for views returns far more than a person means by "a view". View templates ARE views. Schedules and sheets ARE views. So are the Project Browser and System Browser, which are real View elements nobody ever wants back. A plain collector hands all of them over, and a template then gets a template applied to it. So the excluded ones are COUNTED AND REPORTED rather than silently dropped. Asking for "Level 3" and getting nothing must be distinguishable from asking for "Level 3" and matching only a template of that name - the first means the view does not exist, the second means it does and this fragment refused it. A bare zero cannot tell those apart, and the difference changes what the user does next. **VERSION 2 ALSO FINDS SCHEDULES, UNPLACED VIEWS AND VIEWS WITH NO TEMPLATE** (FIND_SCHEDULES, FIND_UNPLACED_VIEWS and FIND_VIEWS_WITHOUT_TEMPLATE merged in). viewType Schedule returns the real schedules - only when asked, never by default - with Revit's internal ones counted in skippedInternal. placement unplaced or placed narrows by whether a view is on a sheet, read through viewports AND schedule placements. withoutTemplate keeps the views no template holds, the ones on sheets first with their sheet numbers. byType counts the answer per view type.

<a id="highlight-vs-rest"></a>

### Highlight vs rest

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** grey everything back and bring these forward.

Greys everything else in the view and gives the elements handed in a colour of their own - the grayout. One subset standing out against a dimmed model, which is what a coordination drawing is for. **Insulation and lining travel with their host, both ways, and this is not optional.** Highlight an insulated duct without them and the duct you asked to see is still wrapped in grey material - it reads as half-applied on screen. So picking a wrap pulls in the run underneath it, and picking a run pulls in its insulation and its lining. Recorded as a standing rule by the owner: if you colour a duct and it has insulation, colour the insulation too, or you cannot see it. **Only what is already in the view is touched.** A wrap outside the view has nothing to override, and adding it would pad the count with elements nobody can see. **It differs from the two fragments nearest it.** OVERRIDE_GRAPHICS_IN_VIEW applies one prepared look to a set and leaves everything else alone; COLOR_BY_PARAMETER splits the set itself into a colour per value. This one is about the REST: it dims the whole view so that one thing reads. **The grey and the highlight colour are asked for**, because a drawing has a house standard for both and this fragment does not own it. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). RESET_GRAPHIC_OVERRIDES is how it is undone.

<a id="insert-views-from-file"></a>

### Insert views from file

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** insert drafting views or legends from a Revit file on disk that is not open, with what is drawn in them, or one view's 2D elements into a view here - Insert > Insert from File > Insert Views from File / Insert 2D Elements from File.

Revit's Insert > Insert from File for a Revit file on disk that is not open. Insert Views from File: each drafting view or legend named is copied into this model with everything drawn in it - the view first, then the elements it owns, as a view copied between models arrives empty otherwise. Insert 2D Elements from File: with a view here named as the target, the 2D elements of the one view named are copied into it at the same coordinates. The file is opened detached with its worksets open, read, and closed without saving; a file already open in this Revit is used and left open. A name the file does not have, or a view that is not a drafting view or legend, is named and skipped. A view Revit will not copy - most often a type of the same name already here - is named and the rest go on. Revit makes "Name(1)" for a view name already here. Every view is counted back against what the file's view held.

<a id="isolate-elements"></a>

### Isolate elements

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-19 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** show only these elements in this view, temporarily.

Shows only the given elements in one view and hides everything else - Revit's Temporary Isolate, done to a set somebody has just found. **Temporary, always.** The user clears it with Revit's own *Reset Temporary Hide/Isolate*, and closing the view or reopening the model clears it too. Nothing here is saved into the view, which is why this is the safe half of visibility work and why a permanent version is a different capability with a different risk. **It resets any isolation already running before applying its own.** Revit's isolate is additive to whatever temporary state the view is already in, so isolating twice without resetting shows the union of both - which reads as the filter having found too much. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). **DECLARED MODIFY SINCE 2026-10-17, ALTHOUGH NOTHING IN THE MODEL CHANGES** (D-125). Revit takes a temporary isolate only inside a transaction, and Heron opens one for fragment code only on the write path, behind the Changes switch. Declared EXECUTE, this card was sent to the show door, which opens none, and Revit refused it there (FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-499). Its `impl/` did not move, so its proof - taken on the write path, rolled back - stands. **With Changes OFF, `revit_isolate_temporary` does the same job** as fixed code in the add-in.

<a id="open-view"></a>

### Open view

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-07 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** put the Level 2 ceiling plan on screen.

Opens an EXISTING view in the active project and makes it the one on screen. It changes nothing in the model and it creates nothing. **IT OPENS, IT NEVER CREATES.** A view name that does not exist is a refusal, not an invitation to make one. Creating a view because the name was mistyped would leave a stray view in somebody's project for every typo, and CREATE_PLAN_VIEW and its siblings are how a view is meant to come into being. **THE CHANGE IS REQUESTED, NOT CONFIRMED, AND THIS FRAGMENT WILL NOT PRETEND OTHERWISE.** `UIDocument.RequestViewChange` is a request: Revit performs it when the current API context ends, which is after this fragment has finished. Reading `ActiveView` back here would report the view from BEFORE the change and call it proof. What is on screen afterwards is checked afterwards. **A VIEW TEMPLATE IS NOT A VIEW YOU CAN OPEN**, and it is refused by name rather than by failing obscurely. Templates appear in the same list and are the most likely wrong answer to *"open the ceiling plan"*. **ALREADY BEING THERE IS A SUCCESS.** Asking for the view already on screen returns success having moved nothing. **FINDING IS A DIFFERENT JOB.** This takes a name and opens it. FIND_VIEWS is what answers *"which views are there"*, and it is what to run first when the name is not already known. Opens no transaction and needs none: it acts on the session, not the building. That is why it is EXECUTE rather than MODIFY. **VERSION 2: IT RUNS WITH NO TRANSACTION OPEN, BECAUSE REVIT CHANGES NO VIEW INSIDE ONE.** Every write fragment runs inside a transaction, and Revit refuses `RequestViewChange` there: *"Cannot change the active view of a modifiable document (with a transaction curently open)"* (Revit's spelling). So version 1 was refused for EVERY view through revit_change - on 2026-10-13 a sheet in Project2 and a 3D view in Project1 - and only its "already on screen" answer ever worked there. Measured 2026-10-13 on Project1, Revit 2020 (FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-456): with no transaction open the same call opens the view, a TransactionGroup alone included. Version 2 declared the ambient `editScopeFailures` need so the add-in would run it inside the job's group with no transaction open (D-112, widened by D-115). Revit's own words now come FIRST in a refusal, because a finding is shown cut short - the add-in cuts every list item to about sixty characters. **TWO VIEWS SHARING A NAME ARE TOLD APART THE LIBRARY'S WAY** - "FloorPlan: Level 1", "DrawingSheet: Ground Floor Plan", the spelling every fragment taking a view accepts. The plain name is tried first and wins when it names one openable view; the refusal for two STARTS with the spellings to use. Run on sheets on 2026-10-13, Revit 2020, before and after (5b-456). **VERSION 3: THE SAME CODE, AND THE SWITCH THAT SAYS WHAT IT NEEDS** - `noTransactionOpen` (D-125) in place of `editScopeFailures`. The write path runs it exactly as before, inside the job's group with no transaction open; and the show door now runs it too, with Changes OFF, because that switch only says "none open" where `editScopeFailures` said "opens its own", which the add-in refuses everywhere but the write path (FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-498). Its `impl/` did not move, so its proof stands. Its code's header still names `editScopeFailures`: editing it would make that proof stale. **THAT PROOF WAS TAKEN ON THE WRITE PATH**, inside a group; the show door runs it with none, and is NEEDS-CHECKING Group ES's ES9 until it has been seen there - so a PROVEN line from `revit_show` speaks for this code, not yet for that path.

### Override graphics in view

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** apply one graphic override to these elements in one view, or to a whole linked model.

Applies a prepared OverrideGraphicSettings to elements in one view, and reports what it could not override. It is the working half of the grayout - grey the background, bring the services forward - and of any other job that changes how something LOOKS without changing what it IS. It takes the settings ALREADY BUILT rather than building them from colours and weights. That is deliberate and it is what makes one implementation work on eight releases - see the compatibility note. **A whole linked model, too** (version 2, from SET_LINK_GRAPHICS). A link is one element in the host, so one override on it greys or fades everything inside it - and a CATEGORY override in the host never reaches inside a link, which is why a greyout on a linked job appears to do nothing. Asked for links only, anything else handed in is counted and left alone; each link's override is read back and named by its file. A view template is refused, and a view following one is warned that the template wins. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="place-view-on-sheet"></a>

### Place view on sheet

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** put these views onto a sheet - or swap one view for another in the same place, taking the old one off.

Places views onto a sheet as viewports. The last step of drawing production, and the one that turns a model into something that gets issued. **A view can be on only ONE sheet, and Revit refuses the second attempt.** That is not a quirk to work around — it is why the refusal is reported by name rather than allowed to abandon a batch of thirty. The usual cause is a view already placed on a sheet somebody else made. **Asked before attempted.** `Viewport.CanAddViewToSheet` is Revit's own answer and it covers the cases that are otherwise exceptions: a view already placed, a schedule that needs a different call, a view template. **Version 3: several views are laid out, never stacked.** One view goes at the point given, or the middle of the sheet. Several go on a grid across the sheet, sized to the views that will place, and `distinctPositions` reads back how many landed in different places - placed 3 with distinctPositions 1 is a pile, and the answer says so. A placeholder sheet is refused by name in `sheetProblem`. **The views may be handed on** (version 3): with none named, the views FIND_VIEWS found unplaced, or the ones selected, are placed; anything handed on that is not a view is refused by id. Views named always win. **Version 2: replace one view with another on its sheets.** Name an `oldViewId` and the one view in `views` takes its place, and the old view comes off - read back in `swapped`, and anything not done said in `notDone`. **Version 4 places schedules too**, as a schedule goes on a sheet - not as a viewport. The point is a viewport's CENTRE but a schedule's TOP-LEFT corner: a schedule hangs from it and grows down and to the right. `placedAt` reads each one back in millimetres and says which. A view can be on one sheet only and the second is refused; a schedule can be on many, so a schedule already placed elsewhere is placed again - Revit's rule. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

The field's own name says which kind; optional, left out means *none*<br>**split into** - text; optional, left out means *none*<br>**segment** - text; optional, left out means *none* |

<a id="read-graphic-overrides"></a>

### Read graphic overrides

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** read the graphic overrides already on these elements in a view.

Reads back the graphic overrides ALREADY on elements in one view - line colour, surface pattern and its colour, transparency, halftone, detail level - and hands the settings object on. Read-only. **IT IS THE HALF THAT WAS MISSING, AND ITS ABSENCE HAD A MEASURED COST.** `OVERRIDE_GRAPHICS_IN_VIEW` takes settings ALREADY BUILT, which is what makes one implementation work on eight releases. Nothing could produce those settings from an element that already looked right, so *"make this pipe look the same as that one"* - a normal sentence on any drawing - had no answer in this library at all and was resolving to `CREATE_PIPE`. **MATCHING IS THIS FRAGMENT PLUS THE WRITER, and that is the point of the split.** Read the source element's look here, hand the object to `OVERRIDE_GRAPHICS_IN_VIEW`, and every element handed to it matches. Neither half has to know what colour anything is. **AN ELEMENT WITH NO OVERRIDE STILL RETURNS A SETTINGS OBJECT**, and it is the empty one. That is not a failure and it is not nothing: applying it to something else CLEARS that thing's override, which is a real use. The report says which elements carried an override and which did not, because "matched to something with no override" and "the call did nothing" look identical afterwards. **What it reads is the PER-ELEMENT override only.** A category override or a filter override in the same view is a different setting, is not read here, and survives untouched - which is why an element can be grey in the view and come back with nothing on it.

<a id="refresh-view"></a>

### Refresh view

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** make the drawing on screen catch up with what was just changed.

Regenerates the document and redraws the active view, so what is on screen matches what is in the model. **NOTHING DID THIS AS A JOB OF ITS OWN.** `Regenerate` is called INSIDE several write fragments where their own next step needs it - after activating a family symbol, before reading back a size - and that is correct and is not the same thing. After a run of changes the view a modeller is looking at can still show the old picture, and the tool reads as broken when it worked. **REGENERATING AND REDRAWING ARE TWO DIFFERENT THINGS AND BOTH ARE NEEDED.** `Document.Regenerate` recomputes the model; refreshing the active view is what puts the result on screen. Doing only the first leaves the screen stale, which is the exact complaint this exists to answer. **IT NEEDS A UI DOCUMENT AND SAYS SO WHEN IT HAS NONE.** A run with no UI - a batch, a headless job - can regenerate and has no screen to refresh. That is reported rather than silently half-done. **IT CHANGES NOTHING IN THE MODEL.** The risk is MODIFY rather than READ only because `Regenerate` can surface a warning Revit had been holding.

<a id="remove-tags"></a>

### Remove tags

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-09 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** take these tags off the drawing.

Deletes tag annotations - and only the tags. It is the undo TAG_ELEMENTS_IN_VIEW never had, and the clean-up after a tagging run that produced more than anybody wanted. **IT DELETES THE TAG, NEVER THE THING TAGGED.** That is the whole risk in this fragment and the reason it refuses anything that is not a tag rather than skipping it quietly. A set gathered by category and handed in loosely could easily contain the ducts as well as their tags, and a delete that took both would be the most damaging thing in this library. **So anything that is not a tag is COUNTED AND NAMED, not silently ignored.** "Removed 40 tags, skipped 12" with no detail leaves nobody able to tell a wrong selection from a partly-tagged view. **A tag is view-specific, so this removes it from the one view it lives in.** The same element tagged in three views has three tags, and deleting one leaves the other two. That is Revit, not a limitation here, and it is said because "remove the tags" usually means all of them. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so a whole drawing's worth of tags is one undo.

<a id="remove-view-filter"></a>

### Remove view filter

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-10 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** take filters off a view, or delete them from the project.

Takes a filter off a view - or, when asked, deletes it from the project entirely. The other end of `APPLY_VIEW_FILTER` and of `CREATE_VIEW_FILTER`, both of which only ever add. **THE TWO ARE COMPLETELY DIFFERENT IN REACH AND THE FRAGMENT WILL NOT BLUR THEM.** Taking a filter off ONE view leaves it in the project and on every other view using it. Deleting it removes it from EVERY view at once, and there is no undo short of Revit's own. So deleting is a separate flag, off by default, and the report says which happened. **BEFORE DELETING, IT SAYS HOW MANY OTHER VIEWS USE IT.** That count is the whole decision: a filter on one view is a leftover, and a filter on twenty is somebody's standard. Deleting the second by accident is a bad afternoon. **A FILTER NOT ON THE VIEW IS NOT AN ERROR**, it is the state somebody wanted. Reported as already absent rather than as a failure, so re-running a tidy-up is safe. **A VIEW GOVERNED BY A TEMPLATE OWNS NO FILTERS OF ITS OWN.** Removing one from such a view does nothing whatever - the template holds them - so those views are NAMED with their template rather than counted as done. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="remove-view-template"></a>

### Remove view template

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-09 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** take the view template off these views so their settings can be edited again.

Detaches the view template from a set of views. The settings the template was holding stop being locked and become editable on each view again. IT EXISTS BECAUSE APPLY_VIEW_TEMPLATE WAS A ONE-WAY DOOR. A template locks everything it controls, `APPLY_VIEW_TEMPLATE` says so in its own purpose, and until this fragment nothing in the library could take one off. *"Why can't I change the scale on this view"* had a diagnosis and no answer. **DETACHING DOES NOT PUT THE VIEW BACK HOW IT WAS, AND THAT IS THE THING PEOPLE GET WRONG.** The view keeps whatever the template last gave it - the same scale, the same visibility, the same overrides - they simply stop being controlled. So a view looks *identical* the instant after this runs, and somebody who asked to "undo the template" reads that as the fragment having done nothing. It did exactly what it says: the settings are now the view's own. That is why the read-back names the template that WAS applied and says the view is unchanged to look at. **IT DOES NOT DELETE THE TEMPLATE.** The template element survives and every other view still using it is untouched. Deleting the template itself is a different job with a different blast radius - it reaches every view in the project, not the ones named here - and it is `DELETE_ELEMENTS` with the template as the element. The earlier library folded that into a flag on this same call; splitting it is deliberate, because a flag that turns "change these three views" into "change the whole project" is the wrong shape for a thing that cannot be undone by re-running it. **A VIEW TEMPLATE IS ITSELF A VIEW**, so a template can be passed in by mistake. That is refused by name rather than skipped silently - a template has no template of its own, and a silent skip reads the same as success. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="reorder-view-filters"></a>

### Reorder view filters

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-20 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** move one filter up or down a view's filter list - to the top, the bottom or a given row.

Moves one filter up or down a view's filter list - the order Visibility/Graphics Overrides, Filters tab shows, where the filter higher in the list wins when two filters set the same line colour, pattern or visibility on the same element. To the top, to the bottom, to a row number, or above or below another filter on the same view. A view template can be named as the view, and then every view following it draws in the new order; the answer says how many follow it. **Nothing else changes.** Revit has no way to set the order directly, so the filters that have to move are taken off the view and put back in the new order. Each one's whole row - projection and cut lines and patterns, colours, transparency, halftone, Visibility and, from Revit 2021, Enable Filter - is read BEFORE anything is written, written back, and read back after. If any setting or the order does not read back as it was asked, the call stops and nothing it did is kept. **What it can check differs by release, and the answer says which.** From Revit 2021 it reads the order from Revit before and after, and a typed `currentOrder` that differs from Revit's is refused as out of date. On Revit 2020 the API cannot read the order the Filters tab shows (from 2021 Revit's reference says its plain list is sorted by id; 2020's says nothing, and is assumed the same), so it needs the modeller's own reading of the Filters tab as `currentOrder` - except on a view with two filters or fewer, or a move to the bottom, which do not depend on the order. On 2020 the new order is WRITTEN, never read back: look at the Filters tab. **Refused, with nothing changed:** a filter not on the view (it says what is, and APPLY_VIEW_FILTER puts one on); a view whose view template controls its filters (it names the template - ask again with the template as the view); a view that takes no filters; an unreadable row number. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="repoint-view-reference"></a>

### Repoint view reference

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** make these section marks open the new views instead of the old ones.

Re-points section marks, callout bubbles and elevation marks at a different view, so they open - and annotate for - the view somebody actually means. **THE JOB THIS EXISTS FOR IS A DUPLICATED SET.** Sheets get duplicated, the marks come with them, and every one still references the ORIGINAL view - so each bubble on the new sheets prints the old sheet and detail number. Nothing about the mark looks wrong, and retyping the text is impossible because the text is not on the mark: it is drawn from whichever view the mark points at. **IT CHANGES WHAT A DRAWING SAYS, WHICH IS WHY IT IS SEPARATE FROM THE REPORT.** Read first with `REPORT_VIEW_REFERENCES`, look at what each mark points at now, then re-point the ones that are wrong. An audit that repaired as it went would change a set of drawings while somebody was still deciding. **EVERY MARK IS READ BACK.** The call can leave a mark where it was - a marker whose kind cannot reference the chosen view, for instance - so what each mark points at afterwards is read again and only a real change counts. A mark that did not take is refused, never reported as done. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so a whole sheet's marks are one undo entry.

<a id="report-category-overrides"></a>

### Report category overrides

**DRAFT - runs in a chat, and its answer says so.** It changes nothing in the model, so it is not refused, but it has not been proved on a real model yet.

**What it does:** which categories are overridden or switched off in this view.

Lists which CATEGORIES carry a graphic override in one view - the reverse lookup for `SET_CATEGORY_GRAPHICS`, which only ever sets - and, since version 3, which categories are switched off in it, the read half of `SET_CATEGORY_VISIBILITY`. Read-only. **`READ_GRAPHIC_OVERRIDES` CANNOT ANSWER THIS, AND SAYS SO IN ITS OWN PURPOSE** - it reads the PER-ELEMENT override only. Yet *"what category overrides are on this view"* was resolving to it, which is a question answered by a fragment that structurally cannot answer it: the worst kind of near-miss, because the reply comes back empty and reads as *"nothing is overridden"*. **THE VISIBILITY FLAG IS NOT THE SIGNAL, AND THIS IS THE TRAP.** A pattern's own "is visible" property reads TRUE on a category with nothing overridden at all, so a check built on it reports every category in the model as overridden. The real signal is a VALID COLOUR or a REAL PATTERN ID - something that was actually set. **IT LOOKS AT THE CATEGORIES PRESENT IN THE VIEW, not at every category in the document.** A model has hundreds; a drawing shows a few dozen. Scanning them all produces a report nobody reads, and the ones absent from the view cannot be why it looks wrong. **THIS IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE GRAYOUT QUESTION.** An element that is grey with no per-element override is grey because its CATEGORY is - and until this existed, nothing in the library could say that. **The whole Visibility/Graphics of the view, with `allCategories`.** Every category hidden, overridden or drawn - linked models included, since an override acts on them too - with each override's colours, line weights and patterns beside its Object Styles; the sub-categories and annotation categories hidden or overridden; and the elements that carry their own override. The view filters are REPORT_VIEW_FILTERS'. **Switched off is not overridden** (version 3, from REPORT_CATEGORY_VISIBILITY). A category switched off shows nothing; one overridden shows differently. Every category switched off in the view is listed on every call - the whole model is asked, never only what the view draws, because a hidden category's elements are in no view-scoped collector - empty ones included and marked so, with how many of the view's rows its template owns and the template named.

| **You get** | findings, overridden categories, override list, model category list, sub category list, annotation category list, element override list, hidden categories, hidden category list |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | none |

<a id="report-filterable-parameters"></a>

### Report filterable parameters

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** which parameters can I actually build a view filter on for these categories.

Asked before a view filter is built: which of these categories can be filtered at all, and which parameters are legal to filter on across ALL of them together. Read-only. **IT ANSWERS THE TWO WAYS CREATING A FILTER FAILS, BEFORE IT FAILS.** A category that cannot be filtered - links, some annotation and view-specific categories - makes the create call throw, with an exception that names none of them, so one bad category loses the whole filter. And a parameter can be present on the element and still not be available to a filter. Both are askable in advance; neither is guessable from the element. **THE LEGAL SET SHRINKS AS CATEGORIES ARE ADDED, WHICH IS WHY IN-COMMON IS THE ANSWER THAT MATTERS.** Two categories that each allow a parameter may allow nothing together. `commonParameters` is what a filter over the whole set can use; `perCategory` shows each category on its own, so the one doing the narrowing is visible instead of being hunted for by deletion. **IT NEEDS NO ELEMENT TO EXIST.** The other route to a parameter id is to read a sample element of the category, which gives up when nothing of that kind has been modelled yet - the normal case at the start of a job, and exactly when the filters are being set up. This asks the categories. **"FILTERABLE" IS ABOUT THE MECHANISM, NOT ABOUT THE VALUES.** A parameter listed here can be empty on every element in the model: the filter is legal and matches nothing. It also says nothing about which COMPARISON is allowed - a text rule on a numeric parameter is refused later, by the create call. ASSUMES NOTHING ABOUT TRANSACTIONS - it opens none and needs none.

| **You get** | common parameters, per category, filterable categories, unfilterable categories |

<a id="report-view-filters"></a>

### Report view filters

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-26 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** the filters in the project and on a view in priority order, which views use each, and why a filter draws nothing.

Lists every filter in the project - rule-based and saved-set alike - and which views actually use each one. Read-only. **Name a view and its whole Filters tab comes back** (version 2, 2026-09-28, FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-248). `viewName` takes a view as the Project Browser shows it or as Heron prints it (`FloorPlan: Level 1`), several separated by semicolons, or `*` for every view carrying a filter. For each filter on it, `filterSettings` reads back the row of Visibility/Graphics: Enable Filter, Visibility, projection lines (pattern, colour, weight), surface foreground and background patterns (pattern, colour, Visible tick), transparency, cut lines, cut patterns, halftone - and whether the cut columns apply at all, because Revit greys them out when none of the filter's categories can be cut. It is the read half of APPLY_VIEW_FILTER. A blank `viewName` leaves `filterSettings` empty and the report is what it always was. **And why a filter on a view draws nothing** (version 3, from AUDIT_VIEW_FILTERS). Each filter on a view named comes back numbered in priority order - the higher one wins - with its categories, its rule and how many elements it catches there, and the four ways a filter can be present and do nothing, none of which Revit calls an error: switched off, its visibility off, an empty override, or every one of its categories hidden. A view template owning the filters - the answer to "my change did not save" - is said once, by name. It changes nothing. **Before this, asking what filters a view has resolved to APPLY_VIEW_FILTER**, which is a write. A question about a drawing answered by something that changes it is the worst shape of mis-routing in this library, and it is why this fragment exists at all. **It answers two questions that get asked before two different mistakes.** *What already exists* stops a near-duplicate filter being created beside one that does the job. *Where is this used* stops one being edited or deleted without knowing which drawings change. **A filter applied to NO view is the row worth finding.** It is either a leftover from a standard nobody follows any more, or one somebody made and never applied - and both look identical to a project that is simply tidy. **Not every "view" Revit returns can answer the question.** The project browser and the system browser come back from the same collector and throw when asked about filters, so each is asked inside its own guard - one pseudo-view must not take the whole report down. That was found on a real model, not reasoned about.

| **You get** | findings, unused filters, filter settings, disabled, hidden, blank override, nothing to act on, template owned |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2020 |

<a id="report-view-references"></a>

### Report view references

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-08 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** what view does this section mark actually open.

For each section mark, callout bubble or elevation mark, reports WHICH VIEW it points at - and whether that view is on a sheet. Read-only. **A MARK AND THE VIEW IT OPENS ARE TWO SEPARATE ELEMENTS, AND THE TEXT ON THE MARK IS NOT A PARAMETER OF THE MARK.** The bubble draws its detail number and sheet number from the VIEW it references. So a mark reading the wrong numbers is almost never a text problem: it is pointing at a different view from the one somebody assumes - usually the original, after a set was duplicated. **A MARK POINTING AT A VIEW THAT IS ON NO SHEET SHOWS AN EMPTY BUBBLE.** That is the state worth finding before a drawing is issued, and it is reported as its own list rather than left to be read off the sheet. **IT CHANGES NOTHING.** Re-pointing a mark at another view is a real edit and it belongs to `REPOINT_VIEW_REFERENCE`. Reporting and repairing in one call is how an audit becomes a change nobody asked for. ASSUMES NOTHING ABOUT TRANSACTIONS - it opens none and needs none.

<a id="report-view-template-control"></a>

### Report view template control

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-08 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** why is this view setting greyed out - which template controls it.

For each view, says which view template it follows and which of its settings that template is holding - so a setting that will not accept a change has a named reason. IT EXISTS BECAUSE *"WHY IS THIS GREYED OUT"* IS THE MOST COMMON THING A MODELLER ASKS A VIEW, and the library could apply, remove and diagnose templates while never being able to answer it. A locked scale looks exactly like a broken tool. **A VIEW TEMPLATE INCLUDES SOME SETTINGS AND LEAVES OTHERS FREE**, and that choice is the difference between a template that governs a drawing and one that governs the whole view. This reports both halves for every view: what is locked, and what the view is still allowed to decide for itself. **THE INCLUDE LIST BELONGS TO THE TEMPLATE, NOT TO THE VIEW - AND THE EARLIER LIBRARY HAD THIS BACKWARDS.** Its own file claimed each view sharing a template could independently exclude different parameters from that template's control, and was marked live-verified. Revit's shipped documentation for `GetNonControlledTemplateParameterIds` says the opposite in its first line - the parameters are the ones *"not marked as included when THIS VIEW is used as a template"* - identically worded on Revit 2020 and on 2027, read off the reference assemblies at both ends. So the answer is read FROM THE TEMPLATE, and two views on one template are told the same thing, because they are. **A TEMPLATE PASSED IN DIRECTLY IS ANSWERED, NOT REFUSED.** *"What does this template control"* is the same question asked one step earlier, and it is the question to ask before changing one. Reads only. It opens no transaction and changes nothing.

<a id="reset-view-graphics"></a>

### Reset view graphics

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** put this whole view's category graphics back to normal without knowing what was changed.

Clears the category-level graphic overrides across a whole view in one pass - every category the view will let go of, without being told which ones were touched. IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE UNDO NEEDED A LIST NOBODY HAS. `SET_CATEGORY_GRAPHICS` already clears a category: an empty override IS the cleared state, and that fragment says so. But it is handed the categories, and the request that actually turns up is *"I ran the greyout over this view, put it back"* - where the person does not know, and should not have to know, which of ninety-odd categories were written. A greyout pass writes most of them. This fragment finds them itself, and that is the only difference between the two - stated here so nobody reads it as a second way to do the same thing. **`IsCategoryOverridable` IS THE REAL TEST, AND IT IS NOT OBVIOUS.** Whether a category will accept an override depends on the view, not just on the category: reading `CategoryType` instead lets through categories that then throw. Ones that refuse are counted and skipped, never failed. **IT DOES NOT MAKE THE VIEW NORMAL, AND SAYING SO IS THE POINT.** Two other things colour a view and both survive this untouched: overrides set on individual ELEMENTS, and overrides carried by the view's FILTERS. Either can leave the view looking exactly as wrong as before a full category reset - so what survives is reported rather than left to be discovered. A fragment that answered *"put it back"* with a bare count of ninety would be telling the truth and still misleading. **ANNOTATION CATEGORIES ARE INCLUDED BY DEFAULT** because a greyout pass sets those too, and a reset that leaves the tags and dimensions grey has not finished the job. Set `includeAnnotation` false to leave text, tags and dimensions as they are. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). There is no dry run for that reason: a fragment may not change and roll back to preview, because the batch it sits in is one undo entry.

| **You get** | cleared, still overriding |
