<a id="set-category-graphics"></a>

### Set category graphics

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** override whole categories' graphics in one view.

Applies a graphic override to entire CATEGORIES in one view rather than to a list of elements - the grey background of a grayout, done as two or three settings instead of as an override on every wall in the building. **This is what the background half of a grayout should use.** Overriding elements one by one gives the same picture today and a different one tomorrow: a wall drawn after the grayout ran keeps its normal graphics, because nothing ever touched it. A category override covers everything in that category, now and later. Pass an empty settings object to clear a category's override - the same trick the per-element reset uses, and the reason there is no separate clear here. **A solid colour wash, when it is asked for** (version 3, `solidFill`). A surface colour on its own tints the pattern a material already carries, and where it carries none the colour is stored and prints nothing. With the switch on, Revit's solid fill is stamped onto the surface - and onto the cut where the category is ever cut - so the category reads as a colour on paper. Off, nothing is stamped, so a grey background never becomes solid blocks. On with an empty settings object, the fill alone is stamped: the switch is the ask. A model with no solid fill is refused and nothing is written. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="set-category-visibility"></a>

### Set category visibility

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** turn whole categories on or off in one view.

Turns entire categories on or off in one view - the visibility column in Visibility/Graphics, not a per-element hide. **This is a different job from hiding elements, and confusing the two is the mistake worth guarding against.** Hiding elements affects the ones handed to it and nothing else. This affects the CATEGORY: every instance in that view, including everything modelled after today. It is a saved view setting, it survives closing the model, and it shows on the printed sheet. It is what a grayout actually needs - rebar off, links quietened - and it is the reason that job is a view setting rather than hundreds of element hides. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="set-crop-box-settings"></a>

### Set crop box settings

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** switch crop, crop line and annotation crop on or off across views.

Switches three crop flags across many views at once - cropping on or off, the crop boundary LINE shown or hidden, and the ANNOTATION crop on or off. Flags only; it never resizes anything. **THE ANNOTATION CROP IS THE HALF NOTHING ELSE HERE COVERS, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT SPOILS SHEETS.** The model crop trims geometry. Tags, dimensions and text keep printing outside it until the annotation crop is on too - which is why a neatly cropped plan still arrives on the sheet with a tag hanging over the title block. **IT IS NOT `SET_VIEW_CROP`, and the two compose rather than compete.** That one SIZES a crop around a set of elements, in one view. This one flips flags, across a whole drawing set. Turn cropping on here, size it there. **THE ANNOTATION CROP DOES NOTHING WHILE CROPPING IS OFF.** Revit ignores it. It is still set if asked - refusing would be worse - but the report says so, because otherwise it reads as the call having failed. **EACH FLAG IS OPTIONAL AND UNSET MEANS LEAVE ALONE.** A batch that forces three settings when somebody asked about one is how a drawing set loses its crop boundaries overnight. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="set-section-mark-visibility"></a>

### Set section mark visibility

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** hide the section marks that point at views nobody will get.

Shows only the section and elevation marks whose view is actually on a sheet, and hides the rest - the pre-issue tidy-up so a plan is not covered in markers pointing at working views nobody will ever receive. Or brings them all back in one call. **THE MARK IS NOT THE SECTION.** What is hidden in the plan is the marker element, not the view. Hiding the view would be a different and much worse thing, and the two are easy to confuse because they carry the same name - which is also how the marker is matched to its view here. **A VIEW IS ON A SHEET WHEN A VIEWPORT POINTS AT IT.** A viewport is Revit's own record of the placement rather than a string it formats, so there is no placeholder to recognise and nothing to translate, and the empty case comes out right for free: no viewport, not on a sheet. This read the view's sheet-number parameter until 2026-09-13 and that is what got the empty case WRONG - Revit writes its placeholder there for a view on no sheet, the placeholder is not empty, so every view read as placed and every mark was skipped. **IT UNHIDES EVERYTHING FIRST, THEN HIDES WHAT SHOULD BE HIDDEN.** Without that, a mark hidden on an earlier run stays hidden after its section is finally placed on a sheet: the tool would only ever hide, never restore, and a drawing would lose marks over time with nobody able to say when. **IT IS ONE VIEW'S OVERRIDE.** Hiding here is per view. It does not touch category visibility or any filter - so a mark still invisible afterwards is hidden by something else, and unhiding through this will never bring it back. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="set-view-crop"></a>

### Set view crop

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** crop this view around these elements, or to a shaped loop.

Sets a view's crop region to enclose the given elements, with a margin, and switches the crop on. **A crop is not a section box and not an isolate, and all three are asked for with "just show me this part".** - **Crop** — trims what the drawing shows, in the view's own plane. This. - **Section box** — cuts the model in 3D. `SET_VIEW_SECTION_BOX`. - **Isolate** — hides other elements, whole view. `ISOLATE_ELEMENTS`. A crop changes what prints. That is its point and its risk: a view on a sheet cropped tighter loses whatever fell outside, and nobody reviewing the sheet can tell it was ever there. **Setting the crop without switching it on leaves the view looking identical**, which reads as the call having done nothing — so both happen here. **Or a shaped crop, from a closed loop** (version 2, from SET_VIEW_CROP_TO_SHAPE) - an L round a wing, a stepped boundary along a match line, the outline of a room. The crop box can only ever be a rectangle; a shape goes through the view's crop-region shape manager. Revit requires the loop to be closed, flat in the view's own plane and not crossing itself, and gives the same unhelpful error for all three: the curves are chained here, a small gap bridged and the worst gap REPORTED, and a gap past the tolerance refused in millimetres. One view only. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="set-view-filter-categories"></a>

### Set view filter categories

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-26 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** rename existing view filters, change their rule, and tick and untick their categories.

Edits rule-based view filters already in the project - renames one, changes its rule, changes which categories it applies to, or all three in one undo step - keeping every view it is on and its overrides there. *"Rename it OUTSEL_TRG_MECH_Level_Grid, add Grids, and make the rule Type Name does not contain ABC_MEC."* **A BLANK KEEPS WHAT THE FILTER HAS** - the name, the rule or the categories. **THE CATEGORIES GIVEN REPLACE THE ONES IT HAD.** One it had that the request leaves out is taken off, which is how "not Duct Systems" is said; adding one means giving the ones it has and the new one. **THE RULE IS WRITTEN WITH ITS OPERATOR IN FRONT** - "does not contain ABC_MEC", "begins with M_"; none means equals. A parameter left blank keeps the one the rule tests now. **A CATEGORY THE RULE CANNOT APPLY TO IS LEFT OUT, NAMED WITH THE REASON, AND THE REST ARE STILL SET.** Each is asked whether it may be filtered by every parameter the rule tests, then put to Revit's own acceptability test for that rule, and the survivors are tested together once more before anything is set. One that no given category survives for keeps what it had - never emptied. A new rule with the categories kept must fit all of them. **A NEW NAME OR RULE IS ALL OR NOTHING.** A name another filter has, or a rule one filter cannot take, changes nothing. **A SECOND RUN CHANGES NOTHING.** What it already holds is reported as already so and not written again. **AFTERWARDS EACH ONE IS READ BACK FROM REVIT** - its name, categories, rule, and how many elements that rule catches today. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="set-view-properties"></a>

### Set view properties

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** set or change the scale, detail, visual style, phase or view range on these views.

Sets or changes the scale, detail level, visual style, phase, phase filter and a plan's view range across many views at once - the light version of what a view template does, for the case where a template is not wanted or does not exist yet. Each property is set on its own and read back; anything not given is not touched; a view under a template that holds a property is refused for it, with the reason. A view already as asked is not counted as changed, and each view's old scale and view range come back so they can be put back. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

ISOLATE_ELEMENTS is the fragment for "show only these"; the two get asked for in the same words and do different things. **The margin is a per-request input with no default.** How much context to keep around a clash is a judgement about the job, and a number invented here would become a number quietly relied on. **Only a 3D view has a section box.** Asked of a plan or a section, this refuses by name rather than doing nothing - a silent no-op reads as a broken tool while the user waits for the view to change. <a id="set-view-template-control"></a>

### Set view template control

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** change which settings a view template holds and which it leaves each view to decide.

Changes which settings a view template includes. A setting the template includes is locked on every view following it; a setting left out is each view's own to set. IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE ANSWER TO A LOCKED SETTING IS USUALLY NOT TO THROW THE TEMPLATE AWAY. *"The scale is greyed out"* almost always means *let the scale be mine and keep the rest of the standard*, and until this fragment the only thing the library could do was `REMOVE_VIEW_TEMPLATE`, which gives up every other setting the template was holding. **THIS CHANGES THE TEMPLATE, SO IT CHANGES EVERY VIEW FOLLOWING IT.** That is the whole hazard and it must be read before the call, not after. Freeing *View Scale* to fix one plan frees it on all thirty-four views on that template, and each of them keeps whatever scale it happens to have - which reads as nothing having happened until somebody notices a sheet at the wrong scale weeks later. So the count of views on the template is reported whether it was asked for or not. **THE EARLIER LIBRARY BELIEVED THIS WAS A PER-VIEW SETTING, AND IT IS NOT.** Its file said each view sharing a template could exclude different parameters from that template's control, and was marked live-verified. Revit's shipped documentation says the parameters are those *"not marked as included when THIS VIEW is used as a template"* - the same wording on Revit 2020 and on 2027. Called on an ordinary view the API does not fail; it records a preference for the day that view becomes a template, and changes nothing anybody can see. **A silent no-op is the worst possible answer here**, so a view that is not a template is refused by name. **THERE IS NO "REPLACE THE WHOLE LIST" OPTION, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE.** The earlier library had one. A list that replaces the excluded set silently locks or frees every setting the caller did not think to name, across every view on the template. This adds and removes the settings named and touches nothing else. **A SETTING THE TEMPLATE CANNOT CONTROL IS REPORTED, NOT SWALLOWED.** Revit ignores ids outside the template's own controllable list without complaining, which turns a misspelt setting name into a successful call that did nothing. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="set-view-underlay"></a>

### Set view underlay

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** show me the floor below while i work on this plan.

Sets - or clears - the underlay on plan views: the ghosted level shown behind the one being worked on. The MEP habit of *"show me the floor below while I route"*, and the reflected-ceiling habit of showing what is above, done across many views in one pass instead of one properties palette at a time. **The underlay is three settings that have to agree, which is why it is a fragment and not a parameter write.** A base level, a top level and an orientation. Writing the base alone leaves the old top in place and the view then shows a RANGE nobody asked for - base set to Level 2 with the top still at Level 5 gives three storeys of ghost, which reads as a corrupted view rather than a wrong setting. Base and top are set together, in one call, for that reason. **The orientation is not cosmetic.** Looking down shows what is BELOW the range - the floor you are tracing. Looking up shows what is ABOVE it - the ceiling habit. The wrong one gives an underlay that looks empty, and an empty underlay reads as broken rather than as pointed the wrong way. **Only plan views have one.** Floor plans, ceiling plans, structural and area plans. A section, an elevation, a 3D view or a schedule has no such setting, and anything handed in that is not a plan is NAMED rather than passed over - a silent skip on half a list is how somebody concludes the tool did nothing. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="set-view-workset-visibility"></a>

### Set view workset visibility

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-08 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** turn worksets on or off in one view.

Turns worksets on and off in ONE view - the Worksets tab of Visibility/Graphics, reached from code. The usual job is *"show me only the mechanical workset in this 3D view"*: the named worksets on, every other user workset off. **REVIT HAS NO SINGLE "WHICH WORKSETS DOES THIS VIEW SHOW" PROPERTY.** A phase is one settable property on the view; workset visibility is one setting PER WORKSET per view, which is why this loops rather than assigns. Somebody expecting one call and finding none often concludes it cannot be done. **A WORKSET HAS THREE STATES IN A VIEW, NOT TWO**, and the third is why a workset "turned on" can still be invisible. Visible, Hidden, and Use Global Setting - which defers to the workset's own default. Setting the ones wanted to Visible without pushing the others to Hidden leaves them on global, and global is usually visible: the view then shows everything and looks as if nothing happened. `hideAllOthers` is what closes that, and it is on by default. **ON A MODEL THAT IS NOT WORKSHARED THERE ARE NO USER WORKSETS AT ALL.** It reports that and changes nothing, rather than throwing. An empty result there means the question does not apply, not that the view is wrong. **This is not SET_CATEGORY_VISIBILITY.** A category is what a thing IS - all ducts. A workset is who OWNS it - everything the mechanical team modelled, ducts and equipment and lines together. Asking for one and getting the other is the mis-route this pair guards against. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="show-analysis-heatmap"></a>

### Show analysis heatmap

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** colour the model by how much, with a scale and a legend.

Paints a gradient over the model from a number per element - pipes by pressure drop, spaces by airflow, ducts by velocity - using Revit's own analysis display, which draws its own colour legend. **THIS SHOWS HOW MUCH; THE OVERRIDE FRAGMENTS SHOW WHICH.** A graphic override gives one flat colour per bucket: 26 l/s and 260 l/s are both "blue", and there is no scale to read against. This interpolates between the smallest and largest value and puts a legend on the drawing, so it reads as an analysis rather than as a selection highlight. **FIVE THINGS MAKE IT SHOW NOTHING AND NONE OF THEM ERRORS.** The view has to be told to USE the display style - creating one is not enough, and without that step the data is stored, no legend appears and the model looks untouched. The result schema id goes stale the moment somebody clears the view, so it is re-checked against what is registered on every run rather than remembered. It only paints FACES, so an element the view draws as a line contributes nothing. A plan paints the faces you are looking down at, which for a pipe is the top of a cylinder and nearly invisible - a 3D view is what this is for. And if every value is the same, the whole model comes out one colour, which reads as broken: that is reported rather than left to look like a failure. **THE VALUES ARE THE CALLER'S.** Where the number comes from - a flow, a pressure drop, an occupancy - is another fragment's answer. This paints whatever it is given, which is why it works for any of them. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** bring back elements that were hidden in this view.

Undoes a hide. HIDE_ELEMENTS and ISOLATE_ELEMENTS could both take things off a view and nothing here could put them back, which made every hide a one-way door - the user says "show them again" and Heron has nothing to offer. **The two modes are NOT mirror images of hiding, and that asymmetry is the whole reason to read this fragment before using it.** A permanent hide is undone element by element. A temporary one CANNOT BE: Revit's only way out of temporary hide/isolate is to leave the mode entirely, which brings back everything anybody hid temporarily, not just the elements named here. So the temporary path ignores its own element list, and says so in `temporaryModeCleared` rather than reporting a count that would imply a precision it does not have. <a id="tag-elements-in-view"></a>

### Tag elements in view

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** tag a mixed set of elements in one view, each with the right tag family, without double-tagging.

Tags a MIXED set of elements in one view - ducts get a duct tag, doors a door tag, walls a wall tag - and reports what it tagged, what was already tagged, and what it could not tag and why. THREE THINGS IT KNOWS THAT THE API WILL NOT TELL YOU, all of them the reason this is a fragment rather than three lines: **1. Which tag category tags what.** For MEP it is a fixed map carried here - nothing in the API derives "a duct is tagged by a duct tag". Every other category takes the tag category Revit's own names give it (OST_Doors to OST_DoorTags). Rooms, spaces and zones take their own kind (version 7). **2. The tag family must come from the project's own default, never from the first one loaded.** `GetDefaultFamilyTypeId` on the tag category returns what Revit's own "Tag by Category" would use - the family this project standardised on. Taking the first loaded symbol instead silently produces the wrong tag family on every element, and the drawing looks tagged. The order here is: the caller's hint, then the project default, then first loaded - and the answer SAYS which of the three it used, so a guess is never invisible. **3. `IndependentTag.Create` DOES NOT RELIABLY HONOUR THE TYPE PASSED TO IT, and it throws nothing.** Measured where this was re-authored from: 38 tags created with an explicit type id all came out as the document's default type instead. So every tag's type is read back after creation and corrected, and the number of corrections is REPORTED rather than quietly fixed - a silent correction hides an API that is not doing what it was told. IT NEVER DOUBLE-TAGS. Existing tags in the view are read first and their targets recorded, so running twice is safe and the second run says "already tagged" instead of stacking a second tag - the failure that makes a drawing look right on screen and print wrong. NO DRY-RUN INPUT, DELIBERATELY. Previewing a write is the HOST's job through the Step 6 preview and approval path. A second preview inside the fragment would be a second mechanism that can disagree with the first about what is going to happen, and the one the user approved must be the one that runs. TAGS ARE VIEW-SPECIFIC. An element tagged in the ceiling plan is untagged in the section, and that is correct Revit behaviour rather than a miss. WHICH VIEW COMES FROM THE REQUEST, NOT FROM A FRAGMENT. The user says "tag everything in THIS view", and turning that into a `View` is the host's job - the same shape as `category` on a filter or the template name on APPLY_VIEW_TEMPLATE. Declaring it fragment-sourced instead made the dependency graph report this action as one nothing could feed, because the graph requires a SINGLE producer to satisfy every fragment-sourced need and no filter provides both `elements` and a `view`. That report was right about the contract and is fixed here by naming the source correctly, not by working around the graph. ONE TAG TYPE ON EVERYTHING, WHEN IT IS NAMED (version 6). Given an exact tag type, that type is placed on every element whatever its category - a Multi-Category tag on a mixed set, or one family chosen by hand - and an element is left alone only when it already carries a tag of THAT type in the view. So "tag the ducts again using this tag family" adds the new family to ducts tagged with another, and running it twice stacks nothing. Risers are still skipped. **ROOMS, SPACES AND HVAC ZONES ARE TAGGED WITH THEIR OWN TAGS** (version 7, TAG_ROOMS merged in) - a room tag on a room, a space tag on a space, a zone tag on a zone, through Revit's own calls, never an ordinary element tag. The tag type is the one named, which must be of that kind or the element is refused, or the project's default room, space or zone tag; it is never guessed. Only in a plan of their own level: one not placed, not enclosed or on another level is named, and every tag is read back. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16), so tagging a whole view is one undo entry.

<a id="test-view-filter-match"></a>

### Test view filter match

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** why is my filter not catching these.

Tests an existing filter against elements and says, for each one, whether it MATCHES, fails the rule, or could never match at all - without applying the filter to any view or changing anything. **THE THIRD VERDICT IS THE WHOLE POINT.** A rule-based view filter only ever applies to the categories it was scoped to. An element outside that list can satisfy the rule perfectly and still never be caught, because the filter was never looking at its category. A plain pass/fail test reports those as "fails the rule" and sends somebody off rewriting a rule that was already correct - which is hours, and it is the commonest way this question gets answered wrongly. **A selection filter has no rule, so membership is the only question.** It is a hand-picked list; an element is in it or it is not, and there is nothing to diagnose. The report says which kind of filter it found, because that changes what the answer even means. **Nothing is applied and no view is touched.** APPLY_VIEW_FILTER is what puts a filter on a view. This exists so the rule can be understood before it is.

<a id="transfer-view-filters-between-documents"></a>

### Transfer view filters between documents

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-08 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** bring the view filters over from the other project.

Copies view filters from another OPEN project into this one - *"bring the filters over from the template"*, *"copy the filters from last job"*. **A FILTER ARRIVES IN THE PROJECT, NOT ON A VIEW.** A `ParameterFilterElement` is project-wide: transferring it makes it available, and puts it on nothing. Applying it to a view is a separate act - `APPLY_VIEW_FILTER` - and expecting the graphics to change on arrival is the misreading this fragment exists around. It is the same shape as a transferred legend arriving empty. **A FILTER'S RULES POINT AT PARAMETERS, AND THAT IS WHERE A TRANSFER GOES WRONG QUIETLY.** A filter built on a shared or project parameter means nothing in a project that does not have that parameter. Revit brings what it can and the filter can land holding fewer categories than it left with - a filter that exists, is named right, and selects nothing. So each landed filter is read back and its categories counted against the source's, and any that shrank is named in `weakened` rather than reported as copied. **A transfer that reports success and delivers a filter that matches nothing is the failure being guarded against**, and it is invisible until somebody applies it and sees no change. **BOTH PROJECTS MUST BE OPEN IN THE SAME REVIT.** The source is found by its title among the open documents. If it is not open, the open ones are listed and nothing is attempted - guessing at a file on disk is not something to do quietly. Linked documents are not offered: a link is reached through its `RevitLinkInstance`, and two links can share a title. **A NAME THAT ALREADY EXISTS HERE MAKES THAT ONE FILTER FAIL, AND THIS CANNOT FIX IT.** Revit resolves a clash through a handler object that has to be a CLASS, and a fragment body is compiled inside a single method, so none can be declared. Each filter is copied in its own attempt, a clashing one is named in `clashed`, and the rest go through. This is the same limit `TRANSFER_VIEWS_BETWEEN_DOCUMENTS` records, for the same reason. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). **The undo it belongs to is THIS document's** - Rule 16 is per document, and nothing here touches the source project.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **You say** | **source document title** - text<br>**name contains** - text |
| **You get** | copied, weakened |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2024 |
| **Capability** | `TRANSFER_VIEW_FILTERS_BETWEEN_DOCUMENTS` |

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.
2. Turn **Changes** on in Heron's **Settings** (Heron tab).
3. In a Claude chat, ask in your own words, for example *"bring the view filters over from the template"*. Say the values under **You say** in the same sentence.
4. Heron makes the change as **one entry in Revit's Undo list**. With **Ask to Keep** on, Revit asks **Keep or Discard** first; Ctrl+Z takes it back.

Other ways to ask: *"copy the filters from the other project"* · *"transfer the view filters from that model"*

<a id="transfer-views-between-documents"></a>

### Transfer views between documents

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-14 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** bring the standard schedules and legends over from the other project.

Copies schedules, legends, drafting views or view templates from another open project into this one - *"bring the standard schedules over from the template"*, *"copy the legends from last job"*. **A VIEW COPIED BETWEEN DOCUMENTS ARRIVES EMPTY, AND THAT IS THE FACT THE WHOLE THING TURNS ON.** The document-to-document copy takes the view SHELL: right name, right type, nothing drawn in it. A drafting view or a legend needs a SECOND copy - of the elements that view owns, into the new view - and missing it produces a transfer that reports success and delivers blank sheets. Schedules and view templates are definitions rather than drawn content, so one copy is all they need. **BOTH PROJECTS MUST BE OPEN IN THE SAME REVIT.** The source is found by its title among the open documents. If it is not open, the open ones are listed and nothing is attempted - guessing at a file on disk is not something to do quietly. **A DUPLICATE TYPE NAME MAKES THAT ONE VIEW FAIL, AND THIS CANNOT FIX IT.** Revit resolves a clash - a text type or filled-region type of the same name already here - through a handler object that has to be a CLASS, and a fragment body cannot declare one: every fragment is compiled inside a single method. So each view is copied in its own attempt, a clashing one is named, and the rest go through. A project with many clashes wants Revit's own Transfer Project Standards instead. This is the first job in this library that the fragment shape structurally cannot do, and saying so is better than a workaround that half works. **IT DOES NOT SKIP A NAME THAT ALREADY EXISTS HERE.** Revit makes a second view called "Name(1)". Read the names back before committing to a big transfer. **A VIEW TEMPLATE'S VALUE IS THE FILTERS IT CARRIES, and those are separate elements.** A template copied into a project that does not have them arrives present, correctly named, and controlling less than it did - identical in the template list, and visible only as the wrong things being shown on somebody's sheet. So a transferred template is read back and its filters counted against the source's; one that arrived short is named in `weakened` rather than `copied`, and told to run [TRANSFER_VIEW_FILTERS_BETWEEN_DOCUMENTS](../../../brain/fragments/transfer-view-filters-between-documents/fragment.yaml) first. **Run the filters transfer before this one** and the shortfall does not arise. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **You say** | **source document title** - text<br>**view kind** - text<br>**name contains** - text |
| **You get** | copied, weakened |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2024 |
| **Capability** | `TRANSFER_VIEWS_BETWEEN_DOCUMENTS` |

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.
2. Turn **Changes** on in Heron's **Settings** (Heron tab).
3. In a Claude chat, ask in your own words, for example *"bring the standard schedules over from the template"*. Say the values under **You say** in the same sentence.
4. Heron makes the change as **one entry in Revit's Undo list**. With **Ask to Keep** on, Revit asks **Keep or Discard** first; Ctrl+Z takes it back.

Other ways to ask: *"copy the legends from the other project"* · *"transfer the drafting views"*
